title: Infection prevention, antimicrobial stewardship and infectious disease screening
blurb: Apply hand hygiene and standard precautions, use antibiotics wisely, run IDPS screening and act on GBS when the waters break.
question: Zainab is 38 weeks pregnant. Group B streptococcus was found in her urine this pregnancy. She phones triage: her waters broke an hour ago and she has no contractions. What should the midwife advise?

teach.body: Midwives protect women and babies from infection in three ways: standard infection prevention and control (SICPs) at every contact, wise use of antibiotics (antimicrobial stewardship), and screening that finds infections a baby could catch from its mother (vertical transmission). In plain English: clean hands, the right antibiotic for the right time, and the right blood tests early in every pregnancy.
teach.cite: National IPC Manual (SICPs); NICE NG15; NHS IDPS programme

children.label: Offer repeat testing

teach.body: Antibiotic resistance is a public health threat, so every prescription counts. NICE NG15: in hospital, take microbiological samples before prescribing and review the prescription when results are available; do not give an immediate antibiotic for a self-limiting condition; and consider reviewing intravenous antibiotics at 48 to 72 hours (continue or not, and whether to switch to oral). Midwives support this by sending the right samples, prompting reviews and explaining to women why antibiotics are not always needed.

Group B streptococcus (GBS) lives in the bowel of 20 to 40% of adults and is the most frequent cause of severe early-onset infection in newborns (onset under 7 days). Because Zainab carries GBS, she is asked to come in now rather than wait at home (NICE NG235 1.7.1). With prelabour rupture of membranes at term and GBS this pregnancy, she is offered immediate induction, not 24 hours of expectant management (NG235 1.7.11).

teach.text: Do not offer a rubella immunity test at booking: rubella screening stopped in 2016, and the IDPS trio is HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis. And for prelabour rupture of membranes, GBS carriage changes the plan from 'wait up to 24 hours' to 'induce now'.

items.label: IDPS infections: HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis

items: Five moments; soap and water for visible soiling and gut infections; gloves never replace hand hygiene.
IDPS offers HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis screening early in every pregnancy; rubella screening stopped in 2016.
Offer repeat screening when risk changes, such as a new partner or an STI diagnosis.
Babies of mothers with hepatitis B start vaccination at birth and 4 weeks.
GBS carrier with term prelabour rupture of membranes: come in now and offer immediate induction.
Stewardship: samples first, no antibiotics for self-limiting illness, review IV antibiotics at 48–72 hours.

summary: You can now apply standard precautions and choose the right hand hygiene method, support antimicrobial stewardship, and run IDPS screening including repeat testing. You can also act on GBS carriage when a woman's waters break at term.

A.q: Which three infections does the NHS infectious diseases in pregnancy screening programme (IDPS) currently screen for?
options: HIV, hepatitis B and rubella
HIV, hepatitis C and syphilis
HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis
Hepatitis B, syphilis and GBS
A.why: IDPS screens for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis in every pregnancy, as early as possible.

whyNot.0: Rubella susceptibility screening stopped on 1 April 2016.
whyNot.1: Hepatitis C is not part of the IDPS trio; hepatitis B is.
whyNot.3: GBS is not part of IDPS; HIV is.

A.q: A midwife has just cared for a postnatal woman with suspected norovirus. Which hand hygiene method should she use?
options: Liquid soap and water
Alcohol-based handrub
Handrub followed by gloves
Antiseptic hand wipes
A.why: National IPC Manual: use soap and water for vomiting or diarrhoea and suspected or known gut infections such as norovirus or C. difficile.

whyNot.1: Handrub is the routine choice but is not effective enough against norovirus and spores.
whyNot.2: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene, and handrub is the wrong method here.
whyNot.3: Wipes are not a substitute for washing with soap and running water.

A.q: Sophie's booking IDPS results were negative. Which change at 30 weeks should prompt an offer of repeat screening?
options: She has had a urinary tract infection
She now has a new sexual partner
She is flying abroad at 32 weeks
She has started iron tablets
A.why: IDPS recommends repeat testing if a woman changes sexual partner, injects drugs, is a sex worker, has an infected partner or one sexually active with others, or is diagnosed with an STI.

whyNot.0: A UTI is not an IDPS trigger for repeat HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis testing.
whyNot.2: Travel is not one of the repeat-testing triggers.
whyNot.3: Iron treatment has no bearing on blood-borne infection risk.

B.q: Zainab, 38+2 weeks, has GBS detected this pregnancy. Her waters broke an hour ago and she has no contractions. What should be offered?
options: Expectant management for up to 24 hours
Review after 24 hours if labour has not begun
Immediate induction of labour
Four-hourly temperature at home until labour
B.why: NICE NG235 1.7.11: with prelabour rupture of membranes at term and GBS this pregnancy, offer immediate induction (or caesarean if planned).

whyNot.0: Expectant management up to 24 hours is for women without GBS or other risk factors.
whyNot.1: Waiting 24 hours is the plan for low-risk PROM, not for GBS carriers.
whyNot.3: Home monitoring suits low-risk expectant management, not GBS carriage.

B.q: Lucy is on day 2 of IV antibiotics for postnatal endometritis. She is now afebrile and improving. Which action best supports antimicrobial stewardship?
options: Continue IV treatment for a fixed 7 days
Add a second antibiotic to prevent relapse
Stop antibiotics without a clinical review
Prompt a review of the IV antibiotics now
B.why: NICE NG15 1.1.39: consider reviewing IV antimicrobial prescriptions at 48 to 72 hours, using her response and microbiology results to decide whether to continue and whether to switch to oral.

whyNot.0: A fixed course without review misses the 48–72 hour decision point.
whyNot.1: Adding antibiotics without indication drives resistance.
whyNot.2: Stopping without review is not stewardship; the decision is made at a clinical review.

B.q: A woman's antenatal screening shows she has hepatitis B. What will her baby be offered?
options: Hepatitis B vaccine at birth and at 4 weeks
Hepatitis B vaccine at 8 weeks with the 6-in-1
A hepatitis B blood test at birth, then vaccine
Hepatitis B vaccine at one year with MMRV
B.why: Babies of mothers with hepatitis B are vaccinated at birth and at 4 weeks, plus the routine 6-in-1, with an HBsAg test at 12–18 months.

whyNot.1: The 8-week 6-in-1 is the routine schedule; these babies need doses from birth.
whyNot.2: Vaccination is not delayed for a test; the baby's HBsAg test is at 12–18 months.
whyNot.3: Waiting a year leaves the baby unprotected at the time of highest risk.

C.q: At booking, Hana says she does not think she needs an HIV test because she has been with one partner for years. What is the best response?
options: Add the HIV test to her booking bloods anyway
Tell her HIV testing is compulsory in pregnancy
Explain the benefits, recommend it and respect her choice
Defer the decision until the 28-week bloods
C.why: IDPS: screening is offered and recommended to every woman, but it is a choice (NICE NG201 1.2.13). Early detection allows treatment that greatly reduces vertical transmission.

whyNot.0: Testing without consent is unlawful; she can accept or decline any screening.
whyNot.1: No antenatal screening test is compulsory.
whyNot.3: IDPS tests should be done as early as possible, not deferred to 28 weeks.

C.q: While suturing a perineal tear, a midwife sustains a needlestick injury from a used needle. What should she do first?
options: Squeeze hard and scrub with alcohol gel
Finish the repair, then report at handover
Let it bleed and wash with soap and water
Cover it with a plaster and report tomorrow
C.why: National IPC Manual appendix 10: allow the area to bleed (do not squeeze or suck it), wash with warm running water and soap, then report the incident promptly so that post-exposure assessment can be arranged.

whyNot.0: The manual says do not squeeze the wound; first aid is washing with soap and running water, not alcohol gel.
whyNot.1: First aid comes first and reporting must be urgent, not at handover.
whyNot.3: Delayed reporting can miss the window for post-exposure treatment.

C.q: Grace's IDPS results at booking were negative. At 36 weeks she says she has a new partner and has noticed an unusual discharge. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Reassure her that booking screening covers the pregnancy
Offer repeat HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis testing
Offer rubella immunity testing and MMR advice
Arrange GBS swabs to check for a new infection
C.why: A new partner (and possible STI) are IDPS triggers for repeat testing, so she should be offered repeat screening for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis.

whyNot.0: A negative booking result does not cover new exposure later in pregnancy.
whyNot.2: Rubella screening stopped in 2016 and is unrelated to her new risk.
whyNot.3: GBS swabs do not test for blood-borne infections or syphilis.

reteach.title: Hands, drugs, bloods
reteach.question: Can you sort every infection-prevention task into one of three boxes?

blocks.body: Hands: the five moments, soap and water for gut infections and visible soiling, handrub otherwise, gloves as an extra not a substitute. Drugs: samples first, no antibiotics for self-limiting illness, review IV antibiotics at 48–72 hours. Bloods: HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis early in every pregnancy, repeated when risk changes.

blocks.text: GBS is not part of IDPS. It matters most at the moment the waters break: a known carrier comes in now and is offered immediate induction.

explain.body: Clean hands at the five moments, and before putting on and after removing gloves. Use soap and water for visible soiling and gut infections; otherwise alcohol handrub.

test.q: When is hand hygiene needed in relation to wearing gloves?
options: After removing gloves, not before
Before putting gloves on, not after
Before putting on and after removing
At the start of each shift
test.why: National IPC Manual: hand hygiene before putting on and after removing gloves; gloves do not replace it.

whyNot.0: Hands also need cleaning before gloves go on.
whyNot.1: Hands are contaminated when gloves come off, so clean them again.
whyNot.3: Hand hygiene is needed at each moment of care, not once a shift.

explain.body: HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis screening is offered and recommended early in every pregnancy. Rubella susceptibility screening stopped on 1 April 2016.

test.q: When did routine rubella susceptibility screening in pregnancy stop in England?
options: April 2012
April 2016
April 2020
April 2024
test.why: IDPS: rubella susceptibility screening in pregnancy stopped on 1 April 2016.

whyNot.0: Rubella screening was still running in 2012.
whyNot.2: It had already stopped four years earlier.

explain.body: GBS colonises the bowel of 20–40% of adults and is the most frequent cause of severe early-onset infection in newborns. A carrier with term prelabour rupture of membranes is offered immediate induction.

test.q: Roughly what proportion of adults carry GBS in their bowel flora?
test.why: RCOG Green-top Guideline 36: GBS is present in the bowel flora of 20–40% of adults.

explain.body: Take samples before prescribing in hospital, avoid immediate antibiotics for self-limiting illness, and consider reviewing IV antibiotics at 48–72 hours (NICE NG15).

items.label: before the first dose where possible

test.q: According to NICE NG15, when should intravenous antimicrobials be reviewed?
options: At 24–36 hours
At 5–7 days
At 7–10 days
At 48–72 hours
test.why: NICE NG15 1.1.39: consider reviewing IV antimicrobial prescriptions at 48–72 hours.

whyNot.0: NG15 sets the review at 48–72 hours, when culture results are usually available.
whyNot.1: Five to seven days is too long to leave IV therapy unreviewed.
whyNot.2: Seven to ten days misses the stewardship review point.
